p.x:
When did people stop dancing? 

I was just on a rooftop with about 200 people, amazing DJ, and I was one of maybe 3 people doing anything with my limbs. At most of the raves and clubs have been to in the past few years, me and my friends have been in the minority for doing more movement than swaying back and forth and bouncing our heads in a distracted way. Wth?! Why are people even on the dance floor to begin with if not to dance? 

I wondered if not-dancing has become the “cool” thing, but that doesn’t seem it. When someone starts actually dancing, the  people around them seem happy, like “oh, now I have permission to bob my head a little more and smile.”

One theory is that [doing anything that might get posted online and then get attacked] has dominated the urban American psyche. 

But I wonder if it’s more due to the rise and fall of various party drugs. Amongst adults ages 19-30, use of stimulant party drugs like MDMA and cocaine have decreased. Meanwhile, use of relaxants like cannabis and ketamine have increased. At the same time, young people are drinking less alcohol, a substance which often disinhibits people to let loose.

Personally, I tend to dance sober, but I miss the dance floors of the 2010s. Maybe the miracle of modern science can invent some kind of new party drug that has minimal harmful effects to get people dancing again. 

Anyway, what do you guys think is going on?

My gut reaction is I would hate the way these parties are framed, although i think they sound super cool and I'm glad people are making them happen and I would probably have a good time if i could go to one

I think I feel a lot more comfortable with concrete rules that can be followed, rather than invitations to feel a certain vibe. Rules like "no talking" or "use your non dominant hand only" are easy to follow, and i can vibe however I want as long as I follow the rules. Trying to feel a vibe is a lot trickier and my first instinct is that id spend a lot of time trying to figure out if I was vibing correctly.

It reminds me a lot of zizeks parable of visiting grandma and authoritarianism, which i will link below. Even though concrete rules would be harsher and more restrictive, they allow for a lot more lattitude within them

I do think vibes flow from rules, but it's harder to predict what they'll be. Cold seat went very well, but it resembled much more of a roasting/joking session than just seriously exploring perceptions like i had hoped for. But I still had a good time running it because I wasnt particularly attached to an expectation of the vibe

Keep in mind I have never been to one of these parties, so I may just be totally off with how they work. Not to mention they sound like fun and I would like to go to one, and id probably have fun. I just think the framing would stress me out. But maybe this is just the autism talking

@xenocosmography pushes back on @AGDugin's claim that the Western-Atlanticist project is Cartesian. And btw, this claim is something he developed from Heidegger, who also claimed this about Western modernity.

He cites the decentralized nature of the technologies that Western cultures have produced, as specifically going against this sort of Cartesian "Great Architect" meme (I'm assuming that he is referring to Descartes' On The Method when asserting that Cartesianism is a top-down approach.

The fact is, that this is the Hegelian conflicted identity in action.

Western individualism absolutely does rely on the sort of radical doubt and metaphysical dualism that Descartes develops. This subject-object distinction lies at the root of the Cartesian method which allows for the development of these technologies over the long term, AND this cherished individualism also lies at the root of the desire to assert that individualism against the Great Architect - leading to the development of technologies which accommodate it.

So, in his pursuit of absolute knowledge, Descartes uncovers absolute contradiction.

I noticed this at the time, as well. Reading his work, I was able to see clearly how he made possible both Ayn Rand and Karl Marx. And I was not any sort of phenomenologist or Hegelian - much less Marxist - at the time.

p.x:
On a long drive from LA to San Francisco, @bencera_ decided to stop building for imaginary users.

He'd spent months building products he thought people wanted. Every compromise left the vision weaker. So he let go and built what he wanted – without the assumptions about user expectations.

He took design inspiration from a video game about an AI that builds a paperclip empire and slowly takes over the world. He wrote an about page as an homage to a Giorgio Moroder song. It autoplays when you open it.

He did it because it felt right and he liked it, not because anyone asked for it.

Ben ended that drive on the right path. From $100k to $1.5M ARR in two weeks. Solo.

Episode 1 of the Solo Founders Podcast is live.
